text.en: About 4,500 years ago, in the northwest of the Subcontinent, people built cities with straight streets, brick houses, covered drains and great water tanks. Walking through Dholavira or Mohenjo-daro today, you can still see them. This was India's earliest civilisation. In this chapter we ask what a civilisation is and what we know about it.

A civilisation is a stage of human society with cities, specialised work, trade, planning, shared rules and a way of keeping records. Civilisation began at different times in different parts of the world. In Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq and Syria, it began about 6,000 years ago and ancient Egypt followed a few centuries later. The first civilisation of the Indian Subcontinent is known as the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation, and also as the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site that was identified.
It grew in the northwest of the Subcontinent around the Indus river and the now dried Sarasvati river, in parts of present-day India and Pakistan, with mountain ranges forming natural boundaries. Its mature phase is dated about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Important cities include Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan and Lothal. Dholavira in Gujarat and Rakhigarhi in Haryana are in India.
Cities were carefully planned. Streets ran at right angles and houses were built of baked or sun-dried bricks of standard sizes. Many houses had their own bathrooms and covered drains that led to larger drains under the streets. Wells were built of bricks and regularly maintained. Dholavira had a castle area with great gates, a middle town and a lower town, and an amazing system of reservoirs and channels to store scarce rainwater, which shows careful thinking about water. Mohenjo-daro had a large public bath. Some say the Harappans had a high civic sense, for they kept the city clean and shared its facilities.
People farmed wheat, barley, peas and cotton, kept cattle and made pottery, copper and bronze tools and beautiful beads and ornaments. Stone weights of fixed sizes and measuring rods were used for fair trade. Seals with animals and a script carry short writings, but the script has not yet been read. Harappans traded within the Subcontinent and by land and sea with Mesopotamia. Lothal in Gujarat had a dockyard. They made games, toys and whistles of terracotta, so adults and children enjoyed leisure too. A bronze mirror and a pot found at Dholavira show the skill of their craft.
Evidence shows no army or weapons of war, so the civilisation seems to have been relatively peaceful, with accommodation more than exploitation. Around 1900 BCE the cities began to be abandoned. A climate change that reduced rainfall, and changes in the course of rivers such as the Sarasvati, dried up farmland and weakened trade. The cities disappeared, but much of the culture and technology survived and passed on to later civilisation, as we see in the beads, weights, toys and drainage ideas that continued.

problem.en: A Harappan trader finds 4 weights of 1 unit, 2 units, 4 units and 8 units in his bag. Explain why standard weights matter.

text.en: Weights are the same size everywhere in the city.

why.en: Standardisation is a sign of organised trade.

text.en: So buyer and seller agree on the amount.
This shows the Harappans had rules for trade.

problem.en: Give four signs that a settlement is a city and not just a village.

text.en: Planned streets and brick houses.
Drains and public water works.
Crafts and trade with distant places.
Seals or writing.

prompt.en: Why do we call the Harappan settlements a civilisation?

requiredIdeas.en: They had planned cities with drains and public works.
They had crafts, trade, weights and seals.
They had shared rules and organisation over a large region.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the script is fully understood.
Thinking the cities ended by war.

points.en: A civilisation has cities, specialised work, trade, planning and records.
The Indus-Sarasvati or Harappan civilisation flourished about 2600 to 1900 BCE.
Its cities had drains, wells, great tanks and standard bricks and weights.
Climate change and drying rivers led to the decline of the cities; the culture lived on.
